Treatise I: the Job quotation is Job 27:2-6, though the edition gives Job XXII. 'notitia oris ejus' has been read as 'odoris ejus' (fragrance), which the context requires. The sentence 'et cum praedicationis innocentia ... praeferendum' is syntactically defective and its rendering is tentative. Treatise II: in 'ex toto corde abrenuntiandum esse commonitos' an object seems to have dropped out; '[the devil]' is supplied. 'cum hac in qua nunc sumus anima resurgere' is odd in a passage about the resurrection of the flesh: one would expect 'carne', and the text may be corrupt. Footnote letters in the printed text have been left out.

Treatise III ends with 'Explicit'; Treatise IV (Against the Pagans) begins a new work, as the catalogue note anticipated. Read 'avia' for 'Aria', 'fures' for 'fores', 'mutuamur' for 'mutuamore', 'Judaeorum'/'Jovem' etc. as evident. 'nihil fit quod Dominus ipse voluerit' lacks a negative or 'nisi'; translated as 'nothing happens [except] what'. 'Confractos restituebant' is obscure (perhaps 'the crippled' or 'the broken in body'). The edition's scripture references are sometimes wrong: 'Whatever you do in word or deed' is Col. 3:17, not 2 Cor. 10; 'Ask, and you shall receive' is closer to Matt. 7:7 / Luke 11:9; the foot-washing is John 13. The quotation is from Cicero's lost Hortensius. Line 5 breaks off mid-sentence ('Why then do you supplicate'), apparently a gap in the text.

The text has many lacunae, marked [...]; some phrases around them cannot be construed and are rendered word for word. Evident misreadings translated as intended: 'Durantur' as 'mirantur' (marvel), 'Dubium' as 'fluminum' (rivers), 'labantur' as 'lavantur' (wash), 'luem' as 'tueris' (protect), 'osando' as 'orando' (praying). 'quorum cultus te honestat' is odd in context; perhaps 'inhonestat' (dishonours) was meant. The Virgil citation after the mention of Jupiter's tomb is badly garbled. The Elijah passage seems to merge into an account of Jonah ('like a faithful ship ... delivered [him] whole') and is probably corrupt or lacunose. 'Sostenes' is very likely Ostanes the Magian, who is cited for the same point by Minucius Felix. The Colossians reference should be chapter 1, not 4. The flood passage (Noah) is introduced after a lacuna. Line 1 and the start of line 2 are badly damaged; only legible fragments are translated. 'Coloss. iv' and 'Matth. IXII' read as Coloss. 1 and Matth. 22. In the Peter passage (from the Clementine Recognitions) 'Cum Caesaris teneat Deus... judicum vero ejus; et potestatum speciem servent' is corrupt; rendered by evident sense. 'Pithones' taken as python-spirits (soothsayers). In 'Paravi lucernam' the phrase 'non derelinquit' seems to have lost a negative or is corrupt; sense supplied in brackets. 'Eritis gentes in caput Christiani' appears to have a gloss ('Christiani') absorbed into the quotation.

Line 1: 'et cernerent' (of birds conceiving without males) makes no sense; read as 'generent' ('bring forth'). 'mundus mundam tetigerit' is taken as 'the pure one touched pure [flesh]'. 'litera erit' read as 'heres erit' ('shall be heir'). Several lacunae, marked by dots in the edition, leave the sentences around them incomplete: the passage on 'For we read...', the one on the circumcision of Abraham, the one on Paul and the Jews' 'sign of salvation', the one on the tomb, the comment on 'abundance', and the one on the Ethiopians. Line 2: the edition has 'non dixit in semine tuo' (Galatians 3:16); it is translated as the intended contrast 'seeds' versus 'seed'. The references 'Genes. xx' and 'Luc. XI' are printed errors for Genesis 22 and Luke 1. 'fons' here is rendered 'fountain' (of peace), not 'font'. Both passages are heavily damaged; the edition's dots are kept as gaps, and fragments around them are rendered literally. 'Psal. IX' for 'You are a priest for ever' should be Psalm 109. 'sub regis nostri Christi convertere' lacks a noun (perhaps 'jugum' or 'imperium'); rendered '[the rule]'. 'Si non facio... Mihi irascimini' adapts John 10. 'creavit me principio viarum' follows a lacuna and seems to continue a quotation of Proverbs 8. 'ex ultro aute luciferum' read as 'ex utero ante luciferum'; 'lolus solum' as 'solus solum'; 'aubis' as 'nubis'. 'lucos' (4 Kings 21) rendered 'groves' (sacred groves). 'princeps principatum quaerens' is odd; rendered literally.

nodes.text: Every word of God, brothers, ought indeed to be heard with full attention and care of mind, but most of all this one, which we are going to address to your charity today. For this is why, having now dismissed the catechumens, we have kept only you back to listen: because, besides those things which it is fitting for all Christians to keep in common, we are going to speak specifically about the heavenly mysteries, which none can hear except those who, by the Lord's gift, have already received them. So you ought to hear what we say with reverence as much greater as these things, which are entrusted only to the baptized and to faithful hearers, are greater than those which even catechumens are accustomed to hear. You should not be surprised, dearest brothers, that during the mysteries themselves we said nothing to you about the mysteries, and that we did not at once interpret what we handed on. For we paid to things so holy and divine the honour of silence, and amid those sacred rites of the mysteries we refrain from the office of teaching, so that by keeping silent we may venerate the more the great majesty of divine grace, which no human voice can worthily unfold. But since it is necessary for your love to be instructed and taught in everything, now that the order of the mysteries has been completed, we set out for you the things we handed on before, lest, while you understand less of the dignity of the divine mystery, you should think it less precious. If you understand it, you will see that everything believed precious in this world is utterly worthless in comparison with so great a sacrament. Let each one of you, then, recall the several forms of the mysteries which, by the Lord's gift, you obtained through our ministry, and what you then received simply and faithfully, now understand with discernment, so that you may better keep what you have understood. First of all, certainly, we anointed your ears with the oil of blessing; but learn for what reason this is done, according to the tradition of the Church, by all the catholic priests of Christ. The entry of faith and of all holy doctrine is admitted to the soul through the ears, and understanding springs from hearing. For no one can come to know the sacraments of faith unless he hears someone preaching, as the blessed Apostle affirms, who says: But how will they hear without a preacher? and again: So faith [comes] from hearing, and hearing through the word of God (Rom. 10). Rightly, then, the organs of that sense, without which faith cannot reach the soul, are sanctified with that oil. At the same time [this is done] so that those coming to baptism may keep their ears unpolluted by every evil and shameful word to the very end, and, as if deaf, may not hear one who disparages his neighbour or one who speaks obscene and shameless things, fulfilling that saying of divine Scripture in which it is said: Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue (Sirach 28:28). And elsewhere: Do not believe an empty report. And again: Apply your heart to discipline, and make ready your ear for words of prudence (Prov. 23; Sirach). So the holy anointing applied to the ears signifies that they should turn away from and flee all words outside discipline, as [words] speaking against the teaching of Christ, and turn themselves to hearing the words of God alone, because, once the oil was smeared on, they have kept their hearing for the sayings of Christ. For the Saviour himself speaks to the Father and glories in the obedience of the people who believe in him, saying: Sacrifice and offering you did not want, but ears you have perfected for me (Ps. 39). For the ears of Christ's faithful are truly perfected when they desire to hear nothing but Christ and the things that are Christ's. Hence in the Gospel the same Lord, when he was speaking of the mystery of the heavenly kingdom, said: He who has ears to hear, let him hear (Matt. 11, 13; Mark 4, and elsewhere). For though it is common to all to have ears, yet it is not common [to all] to have ears to hear. For whoever despise the words of God, although they cannot despise them unless they first hear them, yet because they despise what they hear, are not said to have heard either, since they disdain what they have heard as though unheard. And so these people have ears, not such as are called ears to hear, but ears which hear so as not to hear, that is, so that they despise what they have heard as though, as we said, it had never been heard. Only those are said by Christ to have ears to hear who, when they hear with their ears, firmly commit [it] to the mind, and what they have committed to the mind they carry out in deeds. Of hearers of this kind the Lord speaks in the Gospel: But blessed are your eyes, which see, and your ears, which hear (Matt. 13). And again: Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be likened to a wise man who built his house upon rock; and the rain came down, and the rivers came, and the winds blew and came against that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded upon firm rock (Matt. 7). Again, of those who hear badly, who indeed have ears but not for obeying, he declares thus: Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand; and the rain came down, and the winds blew and rushed against that house, and it fell, and great was its ruin (ibid.). You see, then, how great the difference is between one who hears well and one who hears badly: that is, between him who keeps the words of God and him who has heard them and despises them as though never heard. To the one who obeys and does, wisdom is ascribed; to this one who has despised, folly. The one builds on a solid foundation; this one's building is described as vain and, being without foundation, bound to fall easily. There is stability, here ruin, and great ruin. For no one falls more heavily than he who, having heard the word of God, turns to sins, for which eternal punishments have been prepared. But you, after your ears were anointed with blessed oil, have been marked out among the number of wise hearers, so that, rightly retaining the words of God, that is, fulfilling what you have heard, on the day of judgement you may hear Christ saying to you: Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matt. 25). Do not think either that it was done idly, or without a definite reason in the mystery, that we also anointed your nostrils with the oil of blessing. This is understood to be done so that those who come to baptism may be admonished to keep the sacrament of so great a mystery inviolate and whole until death, so that, as long as they draw the breath of this life through their nostrils, they may not withdraw from the worship and service of Christ our Lord. Hence the holy man Job also says: As the Lord lives, who has taken away my judgement, and the Almighty, who has brought my soul to bitterness, as long as breath remains in me and the spirit of God in my nostrils, my lips will not speak iniquity, nor will my tongue speak a lie. Far be it from me to judge you righteous; until I fail I will not withdraw from my innocence. The righteousness which I have begun to hold I will not forsake (Job 27). But a still subtler meaning is signified in this anointing of the nostrils. For the scent of that oil, which has been blessed in the name and power of Christ, calls you to a spiritual sense of smell, so that you may perceive Christ with inestimable sweetness, not with the senses of the body but of the mind; and, delighted by knowledge of his fragrance, following in his footsteps, you may be able to say what the choir of believers says to God: We run after you toward the scent of your ointments (Song 1). This fragrance the Apostle commends to Christians when he says: But thanks be to God, who triumphs over us in Christ Jesus, and makes manifest the fragrance of his knowledge through us in every place, for we are the good fragrance of Christ to God (2 Cor. 2). Consider how much the apostles advanced by perceiving the fragrance of Christ, and [how,] with innocence of preaching and holiness of life, [they are] to be preferred even to the rest; for while they spread the fragrance of Christ's sweet scent everywhere, they themselves too were made a good fragrance to God. This we desire to be fulfilled in you also, dearly beloved brothers: that when you yourselves have received the good fragrance of the knowledge of Christ, a most sweet fragrance may rise up to God from the holiness of your life as well. Through [our] Lord, etc.

We promised in the first treatise that we would speak about all the mysteries which you have obtained through our ministry and the grace of Christ, so that no negligence might arise for us out of ignorance. But we had regard for your effort and memory, taking care that neither the mind, wearied by listening, should be unable to understand everything, nor the memory, burdened by learning many things at once, should quickly forget and lose even what it had understood. So in the first sermon we spoke only of those things which we handed on to you, according to the ordinances of the catholic rule, before you came to the holy font; and we interpreted, as the Lord deigned to grant, what was signified by the anointing which, applied to various parts of your body, designates various meanings, when we showed that through the oil of sanctification you were prepared for the hearing of faith and called to the good fragrance of Christ, [and] admonished that [the devil] must be renounced with the whole heart. Now, however, we are going to speak of the inner mysteries which were celebrated in the holy font itself. For having given a most certain pledge, by which you promised to renounce all his pomps and works and all devilish fornication, you went down into the sacred font, the font of life, the font of redemption, the font sanctified by heavenly power, and so sanctified that it sanctifies people by washing away many sins. For you should not judge those waters with the eyes, but with the mind. For although the substance of that water is of the common nature of waters, yet its effect proceeds from the grace and power of God, who created waters so that by the hidden power of his might they might wash away sins which are not seen. For the Holy Spirit works in that water, so that those who before baptism were held guilty of various crimes, and were going to burn with the devil in the Gehenna of eternal fire, after baptism might be found worthy to enter the kingdom of heaven. Hence the Lord in the Gospel, expressing the power of so great a sacrament, says: Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God (John 3). In this font, then, before we dipped you with your whole body, we asked: Do you believe in God the Father almighty? You answered: I believe. Again we asked: Do you believe also in Jesus Christ his Son, who was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary? You answered one by one: I believe. Again we asked: Do you believe also in the Holy Spirit? You answered likewise: I believe. We did these things according to the command of our Lord Jesus Christ the Saviour, who, when he was ascending to the Father into heaven, instructed the disciples, that is, the apostles, saying: Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep all things whatever I have commanded you (Matt. 28). But let no one, when he hears Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, suppose that we confess three Gods. Far be that sacrilege from our faith! For we have learned, on his own testimony, that there is only one God. I, he says, am God, and there is no other besides me; a just one and a Saviour there is none besides me. Turn to me and you will be saved, for from the end of the earth I am God, and there is no other besides me (Isa. 45; Hos. 13). And in another book: Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God (Deut. 6). And again: The Lord your God, he is in heaven above and on earth below, and there is no other besides him (Deut. 4). We therefore hold and believe three persons, that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, of one power, one substance, one eternity, one will, and also one deity, and we worship the whole Trinity under the name of one God. To believe in many gods is pagan impiety. And again, not to believe in three persons of one substance in one deity and equality, or co-eternity, is heretical madness, since this authority of Christ, which we have cited, is plain: Baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28). As for our asking, Do you believe in the holy Church and the remission of sins? we did not ask in such a way that one should believe in the holy catholic Church in the same manner as one believes in God. It is holy and catholic for this reason, that it believes rightly in God. So we did not say that you should believe in the Church as in God, but understand that we say, and have said, that, living in the holy and catholic Church, you should believe in God. [And] that you should believe also in the resurrection of the flesh, which is to come. Just as, then, you believed in the mystery of the Trinity, and received one God in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; just as you believed that your sins were to be forgiven, and now believe that through baptism they have been forgiven; so also believe that the resurrection of the flesh is to come, which you certainly promised to believe. For the whole hope of Christians consists in this, that we believe that the resurrection of this body, and not of another, will truly come. And just as we now stand in church before the altar of God, so let us believe that on the day of judgement we shall stand before the judgement seat of God, as the blessed apostle Paul says: We must all be made manifest before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is proper to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5). And this is what unbelieving souls do not believe will come. And there are some who promise with their lips to believe but despair in their heart; they do great injury to almighty God, by whom they do not believe that people can be raised and brought to life after death. But we, who give faith to the divine words, cannot doubt our resurrection. For we believe that God, who made human beings when before they had not existed, can easily remake those who have existed. He who made heaven and earth and the seas and what is in them, and all the elements, out of nothing, how can he not restore human beings, whom he made for this purpose, that they might act in this life in such a way as to be judged by it in the other, and earn either rewards for a good will or punishments for a bad one? For this is the faith of catholic Christians, that we believe we shall rise with this soul in which we now are, having a fitting example of our future resurrection in our Lord, the Word of the Father, who, though he is God and Son of God, or the Word, and according to the substance of the godhead co-eternal and consubstantial with the Father, took on the human being of our nature for this reason, in which he willed to be born of a virgin, and afterwards to suffer and to die, and on the third day he rose again and ascended into heaven, that he might kindle us to the hope of resurrection, so that we may believe that we shall be raised from the dead just as we confess that Christ rose from the dead. Hence the blessed Apostle rebukes the minds of unbelievers, saying: But if Christ is preached as risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? (1 Cor. 15). Hold this firmly, then, and believe what is affirmed by the divine words: that there will be a resurrection, in which glorious immortality is to be given to all the saints who love Christ and do his will, so that they may glory for ever in the sight of God with the angels and the heavenly powers; but that unbelievers and sinners, and those who do not do God's commandments, will rise for this: that their flesh, made immortal, may be assigned to eternal fires, so as to burn for ever and never be consumed by burning. For the word of our Lord Jesus Christ also testifies to this, who declared in the Gospel concerning sinners: Then the wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matt. 25). After you had promised to believe these things which we have spoken of up to now, we immersed your bodies three times in the sacred font. This order of baptism is celebrated with a twofold signification of mystery. For rightly were you immersed three times, who received baptism in the name of Jesus Christ, who rose from the dead on the third day. For that immersion, repeated three times, expresses a figure of the Lord's burial, through which you were buried with Christ in baptism and rose with Christ in faith, so that, washed of sins, you may live Christ by imitating him in the holiness of the virtues. Hence the blessed Apostle says: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized in his death? For we have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be [so] in that of his resurrection also, knowing this, that our old self was crucified with [him], so that the body of sin may be destroyed, that we may no longer serve sin (Rom. 6). Consider, brothers, on what condition the Apostle said we were baptized: that we may no longer, he says, serve sin. For what great madness, I do not say negligence, is it, when you have received the remission of sins through baptism, to want to be bound to sins: that you, who had been made holy from a sinner, should want to become a sinner again from a saint, and after that sacred font, in which one may be washed only once, to return again to the filth of vices? Take care, then, dearly beloved, that what you have received, and what can no longer be received by you a second time, you may keep whole and spotless to the end; and, having once been made without sin, may withdraw for ever from all sins. For Christ, who in his mercy cleansed you when you were polluted and defiled by the devil's persuasion, does not want you, once cleansed, to be defiled again. To him be glory and honour, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.

Up to this point we have spoken of the mysteries that are celebrated either before the sacrament of baptism or in baptism itself. Now we shall treat of those things which, by holy ordinance, are carried out in those already baptized. For when baptism has been completed, we pour chrism, that is, the oil of sanctification, on your head, by which it is shown that a royal and priestly dignity is conferred by the Lord on the baptized. For in the Old Testament those who were chosen for the priesthood or for kingship were anointed with holy oil and by anointing of the head; some received from the Lord the power of reigning, others of offering sacrifices. Thus we read that holy David and the other kings were anointed by the prophets, and changed from private men into kings by the oil of sanctification. So too we read that holy Aaron was anointed by Moses, consecrated by holy oil from a layman into a priest of the Lord. Hence it is also sung in the psalm: Like the ointment on the head that ran down onto the beard, the beard of Aaron (Ps. 132). But that oil in the Old Testament conferred a temporal kingship, a temporal priesthood: for in it the life for ministering was bounded by the course of a few years; but this chrism, that is, this anointing which has been laid on you, has conferred the dignity of that priesthood which, once it has been conferred, is never to end. What we have said is certainly wonderful: that by that chrism you have obtained the kingdom of future glory, and priesthood. Yet it is not I, but the apostle Peter, or rather Christ through Peter, who declares that this dignity has been conferred. For thus he speaks to the faithful, that is, to those who have been washed by baptism and consecrated by chrism: But you are a royal and priestly race, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, that you may proclaim the powers of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light (1 Pet. 2). Consider, then, the honour which you have obtained in that mystery, and beware lest perhaps you, who after your sins were made sons of the kingdom through baptism, should by sinning again, God forbid, want to be made sons of Gehenna. And when all the sacraments had been completed, we also handed on to you the commandment of Christ, both by example and by word. For we washed the feet of each one, calling you to imitate us, or rather our Lord and Saviour himself; so that just as we have washed your feet, so you also ought to wash the feet of your brothers and of guests. We teach you to be not only hospitable but also humble, so honouring those whom you have received into your lodgings that you do not blush to perform the service of slaves towards them. Let no one think this an insult to himself, and, puffed up with diabolical swelling, disdain to do the Lord's commandment; and though he may be noble in the world, let him not blush to wash the feet of a Christian who is poor and contemptible in this world. He who commanded this also did it; indeed, before he commanded it, he deigned to do it. For he set forth the example first, so as to commend the command more easily. For thus we read in the Gospel of the Lord Jesus: Knowing, it says, that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came forth from God and goes to God, he rises from supper and laid aside his garments; and when he had taken a towel, he girded himself. Then he put water into a basin, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe [them] with the towel with which he was girded (John 13). And again: But after he washed their feet, he took his garments; and when he had reclined again, he said to them: You know what I have done. You call me Master and Lord, and you say well, for so I am. If then I, the Lord and Master, have washed your feet, how much more ought you also to wash one another's feet! For I have given you an example, that as I do to you, so you also should do. Amen, amen I say to you, the servant is not greater than his lord, nor the apostle greater than he who sent him. If you know these things, you are blessed if you do them (ibid.). Consider then, dearly beloved brothers, what wretchedness, what madness it is that a servant should disdain to wash the feet of a fellow servant, a disciple those of a fellow disciple, when the Lord and Master of all deigned to wash the feet of his servants and disciples. This comes from nowhere else than from unbelief in the things to come. For if we truly and with our whole mind believed that through these precepts of the Lord, which we keep for the whole brief span of our life, we come to eternal and heavenly rewards, we would not only not blush at fulfilling all the works of humility, but would even glory in them. Commit firmly to your memory, then, what you have heard from us, and what you have promised to us, or rather to the Lord. And let no tribulation of the present life ever take from you the remembrance of your pledge. Fulfil everything that you have heard commanded. Do not become like the people of the Jews, who, when they had heard the precepts of God, rightly indeed said: All that the Lord has commanded us we will hear, and we will do them (Exod. 19); but what they had well promised they neglected. For they pleased God because they promised that they would keep his commandments. Thus indeed we read that the people of Israel said to Moses: Draw near, you, and hear all that the Lord our God speaks to you; and you shall speak to us all that the Lord our God speaks to us; and we will hear, and we will do [it]. And the Lord said to Moses: I have heard the voice of the words of this people, all that they have spoken. Who will grant that their heart be so in them that they fear me and keep my precepts all their days? They pleased God, then, as we have said, because they promised that they would do his commandments, but they displeased [him], because they transgressed the commandments set before them, which they had promised to keep. For of them the prophet speaks, saying: They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him (Ps. 77). For this is to love him with the mouth and not with the heart: when they promise that they will do God's will, they lie with the tongue, and flee away to do the devil's will, provoking to anger almighty God, who does not suffer himself to be mocked. Since he sees the works of men however secretly done, since he hears all the words of one whispering however privately, since he understands and knows all the thoughts of all, he will judge most severely. He does not always punish those who despise him here for this reason, that he has decreed that there shall be a judgement in the future, where eternal condemnation and everlasting punishment is reserved for sinners: there will be weeping of eyes and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 8); where, as the Lord himself says: Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched (Mark 9). But we, dearly beloved brothers, trust in the name of the Lord that you do not hear our words, or rather God's words, in passing, since what we say to you we borrow from the holy and divine scriptures. We hope in the Lord that you will do all that you have promised, with the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ helping you in these holy works: to whom be glory and honour, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen. Here it ends.

It is the custom of the servants of God to undertake every good work, in word and in deed, in the name of Christ, since it is to be accomplished for the glory of God, as the Apostle admonishes, saying: Whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of Christ (2 Cor. 10). Today, with the Lord's help, in the name of Christ our Saviour himself, we draw up our battle line against the pagans and carry heavenly weapons, about to strike the enemies of Christ with the javelins of truth, and to lay low the opposing foes, the camp of unbelief and the useless towers with the repeated ram of faith, following Christ as our leader, that is, the Lord Christ, who through Jesus the son of Nave, the successor of Moses, destroyed the walls of the proud city of Jericho, and through his apostles cast down to its foundations the pride of this world exalting itself against the knowledge of God. Come now, let us look at these pagans and bring their assertions into the open. The pagans say that all things happen by fate, and that prayers avail nothing, supplications avail nothing; and that idols are worshipped for the honour and in the likeness of the gods; or they say that all the elements too are gods and goddesses, and dwell in the heavens, and in the signs, and in the stars. We see, then, brothers, that these pagans and astrologers are truly fools, and that these stars are armed with empty weapons and will fall without delay in this battle. For they think that, clad in the proud and lofty arms of their arrogance, as allies of the Philistines they can throw into confusion the battle line of God and the might of Israel, and they do not think that they can easily be laid low by David's stone. This stone is Christ our Lord, who gave victory to David himself, and with mighty power threw down the proud brow of Goliath, raised up in the haughtiness of rashness. This is our God, this is Christ, the Lord who crushes wars, the Lord is his name (Judith 16), who has always been accustomed to be the helper of his servants who fight for his name and take up battle for the truth. The pagans say, then, that all things happen by fate, and that whatever fate has held or decreed concerning the human race is wholly fixed and immovable, and that prayers avail nothing, supplications avail nothing. To them we first say briefly, as with a single plough of faith and of secure truth we cut round and overturn the whole forest of their error: if, then, prayers or supplications avail nothing, O pagans, and what fate has given or decreed is wholly fixed, as you say, why do you worship gods and goddesses? Why do you sacrifice to idols? Why do you bring prayers, and incense, and victims, why all your gifts into the temples, if everything is fixed and decreed, and nothing is granted or obtained by prayers, nothing by petitions? Why then do you supplicate

But they say: We do these things so that they may not harm [us]. To them we say: How can those harm who cannot bestow [anything]? And that they truly can neither harm nor bestow anything is attested by the guard of dogs around those whom you call your gods, and by the watchfulness of guards. For when thieves find them, they carry them off and, having broken them, tear them apart. You say that all things happen by fate; but what you say happens by fate, by I know not what uncertain opinion, I say happens by the will or permission of God; for God the Father has set all things in his own power (Acts 1), and nothing happens [except] what the Lord himself has willed, or has permitted to be able to happen. Do you want to see how much our prophets and apostles did, not by the power of fate, but by that of faith, and by the help of the most high God, and by the divine might of Christ? See, they restored the broken, whom you say are troubled by fate; likewise they healed the sick, raised the dead, gave light to the blind and set the lame upright; and they asked nothing of fate, but accomplished everything, as I have said, by the sincerity of faith and by divine resources and mercies. You say that all things happen by fate? But the fool speaks foolish things, and his heart understands vain things, and, as the famous Tullius said in the Hortensius: My grandmother used to say what you say, that all things happen by fate; but my mother, a wise woman, did not think so. And we too can say in truth that our grandmother, that is, ancient error and pagan folly, used to say this. For our mother, a wise woman, namely Mother Church, who bore us in a spiritual birth, never thought this, for she knows that the Son received from the Father all power in heaven and on earth. Therefore in his name his disciples did such great mighty works, [he] who also said: Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you (John 16). Certainly, when he said this he was opposing errors and demons, who invent fates and contend that prayers avail nothing, so that God may not be asked and their works be undone. Therefore the Lord drew the peoples to himself, so that faith in God might have the greatest power, and distrust might not prevail. You say, shameless one, that all things happen by fate? You add too that prayers avail nothing, supplications avail nothing? But how much the prayers or supplications of the faithful avail, the sacred records of all the divine books declare, and to those who wish to know, easy access to salvation is granted. Therefore nothing is done by fate, but all things are governed by the providence of the maker of the world.

For concerning idols, or concerning the elements, which the pagans consider gods, hear briefly, brothers, our blessed prophet mocking these pagans for their vain things, and saying: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men's hands: they have mouths and do not speak; they have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear (Psalm 134), and the rest that follows there. I ask you, pagan, whether you would wish to be such as those whom you worship, without soul, without sense, without motion, without any living understanding. You think this, then, a curse. Stop, therefore, worshipping such beings, whose likeness troubles you, and whose worship [you think] honours you. But the pagans say: We worship and venerate the sun and the moon, or the stars, and all the elements. To them it is said again: But all men are vain in whom there is no knowledge of God, and from the things that are seen to be good they could not understand him who is; nor, attending to the works, did they recognize who the craftsman was; but they thought either fire, or wind, or the swift air, or the circle of the stars, or the great water, or the sun, or the moon to be gods (Wisdom 13). If they thought this on account of their beauty, let them know how much more beautiful than these the Lord is; for the Creator of beauty established all things. Or if they marvel at their power and works, let them understand from these that he who established these strong things is stronger than they. And the apostle Paul says: For the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, also his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse; because, when they had known God, they did not venerate him as God, or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened: for, saying that they were wise, they became fools. And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of serpents (Romans 1), etc. So, he says, they thought either fire, or wind, or the swift air, or the circle of the stars, or the great water, or the sun, or the moon to be gods. The pagans worship fire, and call it a god, which is put out by water, or smothered by a throw of earth. The pagans worship fire, which is fed by the kindling of wood. The pagans worship fire, they who will burn in eternal fire. But perhaps they worship lightning: why do they worship these things? For they are driven not by their own motions but by the command of God, as are the sun and moon, the rains likewise, and the courses of the stars, the motions of the winds and the flow of the rivers. They venerate, then, the spirit of the air and of the winds. But these serve the Lord of things, as it is written: His spirit will blow, and the waters will flow (Psalm 147) [...] fire, hail, snow, ice, the wind of storms, which do his word (ibid.). The pagans worship the circle of the stars, perfected by God the craftsman, composed with varied beauty for the adornment of the world. They worship water, which is poured out by the bounty of the Creator for the use not only of men but also of cattle and of other things. They worship the sun and moon, although we see the sun, both rising and setting, run just as has been appointed for it. From this it is understood that no one can run unceasingly and keep at his service unless he is under a Lord and has one who commands him. For neither would the moon undergo increase or decrease except by the will and judgment of the Maker; and the sun, if it were in its own power, would shine with perpetual light [...] to serve, and the stars to follow their order, and the sea also to be held within its bounds. And therefore the most holy prophet cries out, saying to the Lord our God: How magnified are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your creation. This sea, great and wide: there are creeping things without number, living creatures small and great (Psalm 103). This is the Lord our God, of whom one of the saints said: He who hung the heaven in lofty height, made firm the earth with its mass cast down, spread out the seas in flowing liquid, and arranged all these things, full and adorned with their own fitting instruments. When therefore you see [...] The pagans still worship mountains, and trees, and springs, and rivers, where oxen, and sheep, and all beasts graze, and walk, and wash. For their images and idols are covered, with fitting honour, by spiders, and pierced by moths or worms, and inhabited by mice, and trodden on by flies; and they neither defend themselves from fire or rain, nor protect themselves from robbers or thieves. And therefore St Cyprian rightly said to Demetrianus the pagan: Be ashamed to worship those whom you yourself defend; be ashamed to hope for help from those whom you protect. For what could they offer to those who worship them, when they cannot avenge themselves on those who do not worship them? For just as it does not concern them that they are worshipped, so they do not feel that they are harmed. But the pagans say: We worship the gods, or goddesses, who are held to be in heaven. To them we say: If you call gods and worship those whom we hear recited in your books, that is, Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, Apollo, Vulcan, Aesculapius and countless others, and you call goddesses Juno, Minerva, Diana, Cybele, Latona and the rest; if, then, you call all those gods, why do you place some among the stars and not others? For you say that Saturn, Jupiter, Mars or Mercury are in heaven, and you do not say [so of] Neptune, Apollo, Vulcan, Aesculapius and the rest. Or perhaps these committed some sin, and those committed none, and therefore you assert that they possess the upper regions, when rather it is agreed that all [...] men, and [...] from men. See, we know that Saturn, or Jupiter, Mars too, and Mercury, etc., committed unspeakable crimes. Does not Virgil, that chief poet of yours, whose verses you venerate even today, cry out thus about Saturn, saying: Fleeing the arms of Jupiter, and an exile from his kingdom taken from him? Whence also Latium took its name from his hiding place, because he had lain hidden safe on its shores, that is, in his flight he had lain hidden within the borders of Italy. And again he says: [...] to Faunus Picus was father; and he names you, Saturn, as his parent; you are the furthest founder of the blood. He first established in Italy the stamping of letters and the marking of coins; hence the treasury is called Saturn's. And he was a cultivator of country life; hence he is painted carrying a sickle. He, when he was seized by mad fury, devoured his own sons; and he fled with his head covered, so as not to be recognized, and so he is fashioned in your shrines. Jupiter his son, withdrawn [from him] by his mother: an island holds his tomb [...] he lies despised [...] whence Virgil said: [...] he lies [...] island [...] of crimes [...] he mentions briefly, saying: And of Jupiter both sister and wife, and, he says, the honours of ravished Ganymede. See how execrable, or rather how detestable, this Jupiter must be held, who wished to have his sister as wife, to say nothing of his other crimes. Alas! What among holy men are held as names of piety have become foul sacrileges among the gods of the pagans. For what shall I say of Mars, who, born among the Thracians [...] infernal, but [...] is said to possess. So he has no seats of his own, but as [...] and wretched in uncertain, and using no seats, always [...] [...] you say begot sons and daughters, who [were] not from lawful marriages but from unspeakable incests and adulteries, just as they themselves were born; and moreover you do not blush to say that the sun had a daughter, and that the moon loved Endymion. Who of the faithful would not be angry at so great a madness of yours? Who would not judge you, persisting in such things, worthy of every punishment? Just as you also say that Saturn is the son of Heaven, and say again that Jupiter is his son, or rather you lie that he begot Minerva from his head [...] thigh, and many other things [...] For your goddesses [...] you assert to be venerable [...] are bound by the vice of obscenity; of whom you say that Venus alone is in heaven, and you place her among the stars. Why not (I ask) Juno too, and Minerva, or Diana, or the others? Or is it because you say Venus is beautiful that you declare she dwells in heaven [...] of foulness you assign to earthly seats? What are you doing with that most shameless woman among so many men in heaven? What does she claim for herself? Is she someone's wife, or mother, or sister, or daughter? But if she is none of these, and you say she is in heaven only on account of her beauty, she who was a harlot, see how wicked it is to say that criminal beauty is in heaven; and do you not say [so of] Minerva, whom you call chaste and wise? It is evident that you are carnal rather than spiritual [...] the religion which the ancients [...] from you [...] lights with [...] pictures and statues and [...] you delight in such things of yours. Why today do the most impure actors in the theatres, to your acclamations, portray that unchaste Venus and adulterous Mars, and that Jupiter, prince of vices, changed for earthly loves with his thunderbolts, that is, with magic arts, now growing white, now flowing down in a golden shower [...] For whoever have sinned without the law will perish without the law, and whoever have sinned in the law will be judged by the law (Romans 2). And the pagans do not blush to speak of so many gods and goddesses, [and to say] that Saturn begot Jupiter and the others. But if gods were born then, why are they not born today too? Unless perhaps, as St Cyprian again said, either Jupiter has grown old or child-bearing has failed in Juno. Likewise the pagans observe the flights of birds and the cries of crows or jackdaws, and in entrails [...] they inquire [...] that [...] to pass by [...] which threaten [...] to turn aside. To them we say: if, then, what is to come can be avoided by observance, then man is no longer under the lot of fate and of an immovable decree, since by his own choice and caution he can turn aside what threatens. But they say: They cannot be turned aside. Let us say to them again: Why then do you inquire? Why do you celebrate sacrifices in vain? Why do you attend to the cries of birds, why to their flights? [...] you groan [...] Do you wish to know how much prayers avail, how much the supplications of the faithful please the Lord God? Inquire in our books, in books clear with bright truth; inquire about Noah, inquire about Moses, inquire about Jesus the son of Nave, inquire about Elijah or Elisha, inquire about Jonah or the other holy prophets, and the blessed apostles, the disciples of Christ, to whom the Lord gave all that their faithful prayer asked. From there, then, you will find how much can be obtained by you [...] in shipwreck, among the raging waves and the din [...] of storms sporting on every side too, through the perils of the sea [...] trusting in the Lord's goodness, happily escaped the fearful peaks of the towering waters, [...] and who, having poured out prayers to the Lord, deserved to be kept safe with all his own, so that even the storm itself marvelled that, while all everywhere were perishing, one alone with his own escaped as a survivor. Let the pagans say, if they can, what fate could do here: did fate kill all in that flood, or did fate grant life to this one man? If fate killed all, why not him too? If fate granted life to him, why not to all? But truly the power and might of almighty God did this without doubt, who allots punishments to the obstinate and the contemptuous, and salvation to the righteous and to those who keep his precepts [...] shall I say [of him] who is known to have fallen short of his master Moses in no merit of virtue, and who, having set out to conquer the city of Jericho, by his prayers, as if by a thunderbolt, threw down the walls of Jericho without delay and laid them level to the foundations; who also held back the most rapid course of the sun over Gibeon by praying (Joshua 10), and checked the paths of the moon over the battle lines by his prohibition, until he should overcome all his adversaries? What shall I say of the most holy Elijah, who by the merit of faith carried the key of the rains on his lips, of which shut [...] of the shipwrecked did not cease from the expectation; he received from the Lord whatever he asked, and like a faithful ship it was kept safe, and, brought to the shore, it delivered [him] whole as it had received [him]. All the holy prophets also, by the merit of their faith, as we said, accomplished many mighty works and many marvels. The blessed apostles too both restored those broken in strength, and asked nothing of fate, and cured the sick, and raised the dead; but they accomplished all things by the power of God and the help of Christ [...] most beloved, let us say [...] of our faith [...] let us speak: one is [...] the Lord God, and holy is [...] saying [...] can [...] since he alone has power, this one God the Church believes and venerates, who forms all things whatsoever that exist by the word of his majesty and by wisdom, and completes them by reason and almighty power. He cannot be seen: he is brighter than sight; nor be reckoned: he is greater than sense; and therefore we reckon him worthily when we call him beyond reckoning. This, I say, is the Lord our God, whom even the philosophers of the pagans, themselves overcome by reason, acknowledge as God, even if they do not venerate him. They do not venerate him for this reason, that to the injury of the Creator himself they assert many gods and, as we said, give the honour of the Creator to the creature. So now even the philosophers themselves, willing or unwilling, pressed by truth, assert our Lord God to be both invisible and all-powerful; on which the eminent Sostenes denies that the form of this world can be seen, and says that true angels stand by his throne; on which Plato too agrees with like reason, and, preaching one God, calls the rest angels or demons. Hermes Trismegistus also acknowledges one God, and confesses him invisible and incomprehensible. Him, then, we confess in truth, and know, and acknowledge: the almighty God, whose work is the world, who hung the heaven like a vault, who founded the earth upon the water, spread out the seas in flowing liquid; and he, the maker, himself holds together the whole mass of this world, composed on every side in wondrous balance. He [...] the heat-bearing [...] of the sun [...] he kindly and usefully prepared all living creatures with all their offspring; he the springs and rivers and hollow torrents; he the wide sea [...] plains [...] with waves far and wide [...] and all things visible and invisible [...] he accomplished through Christ his Son our Lord, as it is written that in Christ all things were created, as the apostle Paul attests, which are in heaven and which are on earth, visible and invisible (Colossians 4). Therefore one God, brothers, alone is to be adored, as it is written: You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve (Matthew 4); he is to be loved, as Scripture says: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your understanding, and your neighbour as yourself (Matthew 22). For who, I ask, is our neighbour, but our Lord Jesus Christ, who, though he was established in the form of God, took the form of a servant? And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt in us (John 1); and he it was who said: This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17). This Jesus Christ [...] in the beginning was the Word with God [...] by the Sibyl ΙΧΘΥΣ, a Greek name, which means fish, [he] worked, because he was to enter the sea of the world or of this age. For consider too the great mystery of the Greek letters themselves, ΙΧΘΥΣ: I iota, that is Jesus; X chi, that is Christos; Θ theta, Theou; Y Yios; Σ sigma, Soter; which is explained in Latin as Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour. In the heads of these five Greek letters is this mystery; it is to be sought, then, with great [...] concerning the Lord Christ the blessed Peter himself [...] discourse, whether one is willing to receive the true prophet or not [...] his, that is, the commandments [...] has in his power. We are, he says, of free will; if this were [not so], those hearing him would not have it in their power to do other than what they had heard; there would be a certain force of nature, through which one would not be free to move to another opinion; or again, if of those hearing none at all received [him], this too would be a force of nature, which compelled one thing to happen, and to the other side [...] because free [...] wishes to turn aside to [one] side [...] his own, and which [...] way it is agreed [...] For from the beginning, while kingdoms [...] and gave power [...] of men; so that one becomes a portion of that kingdom to which he has subjected himself to obey; and since it is determined with God that one man cannot be the servant of both kingdoms, strive with all zeal to hasten into the covenant and laws of the good king. For this reason, then, the true prophet, when he was present with us and saw some of the rich negligent of the worship of God, disclosed this matter thus [...] and the rest; up to this point Saint Peter continues. Christ, then, said: This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17); in this knowledge, brothers, is eternal life. For hear the Scripture of the holy Gospels speaking of the highest God the Father and of his Son Jesus Christ: In the beginning, it says, was the Word, that is the Son, and the Word was with God (John 1), with his begetter [...] in what follows [...] saying, And the Word was made flesh, as a veil [...] interpreter [...] he taught the will of the Father, and handed on that the highest God himself is to be believed, and so, his passion completed, he offered to the Father as a sacrifice the very man whom he had assumed, making the redemption of the whole world. Again we insert the exposition of Saint Peter: And know, he says, the truth, and be separated [...] to deceive [...] writings [...] of the gods [...] For just as one [...] has many under him, you say, for example, prefects, consuls, tribunes and other powers, we think similar things: that, since there is one God greater than all, these gods too are ordered in this world after the likeness of those powers we have mentioned, subject indeed to the greater one, yet dispensing [things] to us, since they are in this world. Hear, then, in answer to this, you pagans, how in the very things you put forward for deception you confess [them] by the reasonings of truth. For you say: As God holds the [place] of Caesar, those who are called gods keep the appearance of his judges and powers. Keep, then, as you have proposed, the example of Caesar; and know that, just as it is lawful for none of the judges or administrators, that is prefects, or proconsuls, or generals, or tribunes, to have the name of Caesar given him—otherwise both he who accepted it and those who conferred it will perish alike—so you ought to consider this matter too. For if anyone gives the name of God to anyone besides him, and that one accepts it, they will meet one and the same destruction, perhaps much worse than the servants of Caesar. For he who offends against Caesar will suffer a temporal destruction; but he who offends against the one who alone is true God [...] forever [...] Other pagans say: We do even better, who give thanks both to the highest God himself and to all [who are] with him. To them it must be said: This is as if a sick man should call both a physician and a poisoner for his cure, when the poisoners can indeed harm, and [the physician] can cure. But the true physician refuses to mix his medicines with their poisons, lest either the harm [...] to the good or health [...] of the world [...] bestows [...] of his pain light [...] and the other elements render service. Finally [...] against the goodness of the Creator the elements, wearied by the crimes of the impious, are overcome; hence it is that either the fruit of the earth is spoiled, or the mildness of the air is disturbed, or the heat of the sun is kindled beyond measure, or an immense force of rains or frosts is poured out. In [...] and the face of death runs about in various forms; for creation would hastily be moved to vengeance against the impious; yet the goodness of God restrains it and reins it in from indignation at the impious, and [bids it] obey his mercy rather than be inflamed by the sins and crimes of men. For the patience of God awaits the conversion of men while they are in this body; but if they persist in impiety to the end of life, then the soul, departing, which is immortal, pays immortal penalties for its persistence in impiety. But we, says holy Peter himself—whose disputation we have taken from the history of blessed Clement his disciple and joined to our words in support—we, then, he says, have been sent for this, that we may disclose to you the lurking places of the ancient serpent, and, dissolving the enmity, reconcile you to God [...] and may it please him [...] but perhaps [...] to care for nothing, and to God [...] we can come to knowledge, how [...] he conducts human affairs [...] to be of God [...] for unless by power [...] they would never serve inferiors, and by this he is shown to have not only care for men but also a certain great affection, for whose service he has bound over such splendid elements. But you will say: What harm is done to God if these too are worshipped by us, if any of you [...] honour [...] or other [...] is not God [...] you were unwilling to apply your mind to examine the things you could easily have grasped, it is certain that you are hindered in the knowledge of God not by the fault of impossibility but of sloth. For if you had wished, from these very useless images you would surely have received a way of understanding [...] to harm [...] with demons leading astray, so that as if wondrous [...] they performed useful things [...] statues walk [...] bronze dogs, and stones [...] fire produced through the air, changed into various shapes, and the rest, which we have heard that Simon the Magus or others did; for Jannes and Mambres also worked magic against Moses [...] to the devil for a time to do some things to lead astray unbelievers, so that [...] in faith [...] the mind of the faithful, and may perfect [itself] in love and fear of God, and not be overcome by evil [...] [...]. And pythons speak future and hidden things, and [...] by worship sometimes [...] tell future and hidden things; they do these things not by divinity but by malice or curiosity; therefore, as has been said, in order to lead astray, in order to deceive; they are wandering and insincere spirits, flying about and prying. For truly those are holy servants and truly ministers of God who work signs of salvation, give life to the dead, and put demons to flight: hence they are truly recognized as belonging to God, by whose light they illuminate the blind, by whose power they heal the sick, by whose mercy they raise the dead, who in the name of Christ, after his likeness, both do and have done many things by the power of faith. Let us therefore pursue their charity, follow their innocence, so that we may keep their gentleness and mildness, and, aided by the everlasting God, may ever render honour and eternal praises to his eternal and blessed Son, adoring and confessing the Father and the Son himself in the Holy Spirit, to whom be glory and majesty forever. Amen. Thanks be to God, always.

The Jews speak according to the letter, not according to [...] reason urges us [...] brothers, a little [...] against the Jews, or [...] with them with your holiness [...] and first I must show this: that this people from the beginning of the world is rejected by divine Providence, and the following people is chosen and taken up from the Gentiles, that is, the Christian people; and so that what we say may be more surely proved, let us begin from the first man himself, Adam. Adam begot Cain and Abel. Cain, the elder by birth, signified the people of the Jews. He is rejected for his crime, and Abel, the younger by birth, is taken up, who represented the Christian people; for God rejected the sacrifices of Cain and accepted the sacrifice of Abel. Abel himself is killed by Cain; and another son of Adam is born in his place, named Seth. Consider the mystery. Abel is interpreted as mourning, Seth as resurrection. So in these two younger brothers [...] because he is commanded both to leave his former errors and old vices, and to go out from there, and to be made into a great nation, that is, into the faithful Christian people spread over the whole world; whence Scripture announced, saying: You shall be nations at the head—the Christians—but the unbelieving people at the tail, that is, the Jews. Abraham begot two sons, Ishmael and Isaac. Ishmael, the elder by birth, was from the slave woman Hagar; Isaac, the younger by birth, from the free woman Sarah; which our apostle Paul, who himself had believed from among the Jews, expressed, saying: We are no longer children of the slave woman but of the free (Galatians 4). [...] you see that the former is rejected and the following one taken up; and Jacob himself blesses the sons of Joseph, his younger son. Now you understand that in Joseph too, the younger son, he shows the Christian people. Jacob therefore blesses those two boys, and places his left hand, that is the sinister one, on the head of the elder, and the right on the head of the younger, to show that the younger would be more honourable and greater. Moses too receives the tablets, and because of the people's guilt threw them down; a second time he receives others written and keeps them, and in the sacred volumes [...] a Prophet from your nation and from your brothers; hear him as [you hear] me. For it shall be: every soul that does not go to that prophet shall perish from its people (Deuteronomy 18). He called Christ a prophet, because he is the prophet of his Father and God. But he is Lord and God of every creature: of him Moses said again in the book of Genesis (chapter 1): In the beginning God made heaven and earth; here touching on the Son as the beginning, in whom God the Father made heaven and earth; which our apostle Paul, attesting Moses' account, expressed, saying that in Christ were created all things that are in the heavens and that are on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions (Colossians 1), and the rest that follows there. In the beginning, then, God made heaven and earth. The beginning is Christ, who said through Solomon: The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works (Proverbs 8) [...] or the world was founded [...] he prepared heaven [...] Christ the Lord, the Son of God, is himself [...] said [...] Firmament, and the firmament was made; let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth; and he made two lights, the greater and the lesser: the greater light for the beginning of the day, and the lesser light for the beginning of the night (Genesis 1). So God spoke and God made. Hear further, God says: Let us make man in our image and likeness; and God made man, in the image of God he made him (Genesis 1). Perhaps the Jew says: God spoke to the angels. He is refuted by the words, and God made man; for it did not say, the angels made, but God, it says, made man. God spoke and God made; that is, the Father commanded and the Son fulfilled. And consider also what is written (Genesis 18) of Abraham, that God appeared to him at the oak of Mamre; and afterwards Scripture has (ibid.), at the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah, that the Lord rained fire and sulphur from the Lord upon those cities. Therefore there is a Father and a Son, from which Father, that is, at whose command, the Son rained fire and sulphur. In the Son, then, God made heaven and earth, he who was before heaven and earth: were not angels, archangels, and all spiritual virtues and powers made before? So when it says, In the beginning God made heaven and earth, it is declared to have said [it] of Christ, in whose person David also said: By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the spirit of his mouth (Psalm 32); this is the Son of God, of whom David himself said again in the second psalm: The Lord said to me: You are my Son, today I have begotten you. See the second mystery: in the second psalm this is said [...] second Son [...] but day [...] most certainly God [begot] the Son, whom he begot not as men do, but as it befitted God to beget, impassibly, incorruptibly, from himself: one begot one, alone alone, God God, king king, unbegotten unbegotten, Father Son, author Word, creator creator, eternal eternal, Spirit Spirit, light light, splendour splendour, holy holy, good good, merciful merciful, perfect perfect. To this Son David again spoke, saying: Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you (Psalm 44). See that, speaking to God, he said to him: God, your God, has anointed you, that is, your Father has anointed you the Son with that ointment of eternal joy, of the eternal sacrament and heavenly mystery; or further [...] The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand (Psalm 109) [...] this king had a Lord, to whom his Lord God had said: Sit at my right hand. Who is this Lord to whom God the Father had spoken, but our Lord Christ his Son? For hear again the Father saying of his Christ: I have prepared a lamp for my Christ; I will clothe his enemies with confusion (Psalm 131). I have prepared a lamp for my Christ, that is, the Church shining and burning with his light, the number of the faithful, which, having received in the heart the light of truth and belief, does not [fail to] abandon the darkness of unbelief and ignorance. I have prepared a lamp for my Christ: again we understand it to be said of holy John, a lamp illuminating the people about this Lord and Saviour and about his coming in the flesh that was to be. And most holy Isaiah said: Be strengthened, he says, you slack hands and feeble knees; and a little after he says: Our God will render judgement; he will come, he will save us: then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will hear (Isaiah 35), and the rest. And Baruch said of Christ: This is our God, no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found every way of prudence, and gave it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved; after this he was seen on earth and lived among men (Baruch 3): so that it was not God the Father who was seen and lived among men, but the Son of God, of whose coming in the incarnation Isaiah again announced, saying: God has revealed that holy arm of his in the sight of all the nations, and all the nations shall see him upon the earth, the salvation from God (Isaiah 52). And yet further he repeats it again and says: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb, and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted, God with us (Isaiah 7). God with us, that is, God in man, the Word in flesh, majesty in a body. He came down like rain upon a fleece (Psalm 71); not with display, not with noise; but the heavenly king entered the world humble. Intending to give the triumphs of immortality and peace to all, he took on a human body, so that for a time he might shade his brightness through the veil of the body, and God might speak to man through man as interpreter. In that temple of the body was God, so that he might make mortal man immortal. But the Jew does not believe, nor does the pagan either, nor do they believe that a virgin gave birth without union with a man. Let them hear and believe, concerning the Saviour's birth from a virgin, that the holy angel sent by God the Father said to the most holy Virgin Mary herself: The Holy Spirit, he says, will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and therefore what will be born of you will be called holy, the Son of God (Luke 2). That immaculate Spirit, that is, the Son of God, pure, holy, secure in himself, took human flesh from holy Mary, and made flesh for himself by his own power and ability. For if he granted this to certain birds, that they conceive from wind or from dust without males, and bring forth, how much more could he himself, as has been said, fashion a body for himself; and if again birds bring forth living chicks from eggs by the overshadowing of their wings, and the earth without intercourse produces certain living creatures, such as worms and the rest, how much more could God in wondrous ways build among men the temple of his own body: he who, had he wished, could have made himself a body even out of stone, or wood, or water, or earth, inasmuch as he had also formed the first man Adam from the slime of the earth; [but he chose] to take on human flesh, so as to show that he had come for the sake of men. For he willed to be born in our likeness, and to die and rise again, for this reason: to show in himself that we too both die and rise again, and to show us the hope of the future resurrection. But the Jew says: So God had to be born of a woman. The flesh of Christ, which God made, was given from a woman, and the majesty of Christ cannot be polluted in the flesh; for if the shining sun is not defiled by any touch whatever, much more could the Lord of the sun not be defiled, even though the pure one touched pure [flesh]. We have him as the leader of our journey, because he is the way to the Father; as the prince of light, because he is the truth, who has poured into us the light of truth; as the author of salvation, because what was made in him is life, who with the Father gives life to all things: through him we always give thanks to God the Father, brothers. But the unbelieving Jews still dare at times to wish to disparage the Christian faith and to insult the faithful people of God; so we must once more go through the divine books, which may confound them with open truth, so that they may understand plainly that they are without hope and without faith. These are the Jews whom holy Stephen rebuked with a clear voice, saying: Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers [did], so do you also. For which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of this Just One, and you are his betrayers and murderers (Acts 7). This holy Stephen says; and of them the blessed apostle Paul also says: Always learning, and never arriving at the knowledge of the truth. For as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupt in mind, reprobate in understanding (2 Timothy 3). For they say: We have circumcision, and we are sons of Abraham; to whom the Lord rightly said: If you were sons of Abraham, you would surely do the works of Abraham. We have circumcision, they say; to whom we say: Would that you had the fragrance of Abraham's faith, and not of your own faithlessness! You are rather sons of vipers, carrying poison within yourselves: you who bring death upon your parents, and by the very act by which you kill others, prepare destruction for yourselves. Of you, O Jews, the prophet David says: They have gone astray from the womb, they have spoken falsehoods. Their wrath is after the likeness of a serpent (Psalm 57). And our apostle Paul says: Whose god is the belly, and [whose] glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things (Philippians 3). So they went astray from the womb, they spoke falsehoods, their wrath is after the likeness of a serpent: you who, shedding with viper bites the vitals and blood of your parents, and sliding away on the slipperiness of your crime, were rolling in the wounds of others; and who, by despising the precepts of the law through various faults of crimes, have fallen with different falls as if over many precipices. See now, if you can, how foul and how shameful is he who stains himself with the blood of others. For we read ...... that no ..... contains understanding of my light, nor through ... shows, the Lord says to them: You are born of the devil as your father, and you wish to do the desires of your father (John 8). For the devil too, changed into a serpent, with deceitful tongues, deceived with factious malice the pious and untutored innocence of the new human beings in paradise: whose madness these too have followed, a serpentine generation, still now trying to deny Christ the Son of God. Against them, with the help of the Lord Christ himself, we have undertaken this disputation; and to them it must still be said: [why] do you take it upon yourselves to call Abraham your father, and assert that you have received his circumcision? Abraham was justified by faith, not by circumcision. For thus the Scripture says: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God (Romans 4). So Abraham was not justified by circumcision, but by faith. For he believed the word of God, and was justified, and obtained a blessing from God, both he and the seed of his faith. For consider, lest you think circumcision is the sign of the faithful: before Abraham all the saints were uncircumcised, and pleased the Lord by purity of mind, and showed in themselves rather the Christian people. Run through the order set down in the sacred Letters, and you will find that all is as we say. First Adam himself, who was formed by the hands of God, remained uncircumcised; then righteous Abel. Enos and Enoch, Noah and Melchizedek, priest of the most high God: all righteous, and they were neither circumcised according to the flesh, as we say, nor had distinctions of foods. For as to Abraham, in that he is said to have received circumcision, that circumcision does not carry the reward of salvation, but had been given as a sign of the race ............... ................. ................. Israel, secondly ...... had already first circumcised ..... but it must be understood spiritually, because through the law, that is, through the precepts of the law, one must be circumcised from the worship of idols, and secondly be circumcised through the Gospel. The Jews say further: We are sons of Abraham; to whom we say: You are sons of Abraham, but from the slave woman, of whom it is written: Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman (Genesis 21, Galatians 4); we, in the glory of God, are sons of the free woman. Ishmael is your father, from whom you derive your race: our father is Isaac, from whom we derive our race. In Isaac, he says, shall your seed be called; that most holy Isaac, whom to his longing parents ........... .............. of whom it is said: For in your seed shall all nations be blessed (Genesis 22); he did not say in your seeds [but in your seed], which is Christ. This is the most holy Isaac, who was led patiently to be a victim, the chief offspring of a most merciful father; who, as we have said, bearing the image of Christ, neither contradicted his father's command nor refused to become the victim. So he is proved to be our father; your mother is Jerusalem, the earthly city; our mother is Jerusalem, the heavenly city; that one is yours, which has perished; this one is ours, which remains forever; you are the earlier, we the later; because Ishmael too was earlier, then Isaac: because those who are first [shall be] last, and those who are last first. It is written: You shall be nations at the head, but the unbelieving people at the tail (Deuteronomy 28). For Isaac himself also begot two sons, Esau and Jacob, of whom it had been said by divine answer to Rebecca, Isaac's wife: Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly; and people shall overcome people, and the elder shall serve the younger; for Jacob, I say, I have loved, but Esau I have hated (Genesis 25). But this has already been mentioned above; for Jacob himself too is described as having had two wives, one Leah, the elder by birth, weak of eyes; the other Rachel, the younger, beautiful. That Leah bore the figure of the Synagogue, weak, as was said, of eyes. Why weak of eyes? Because the sight of the Synagogue was languishing, and it often lamented itself in its unbelieving sons. But this Rachel bore the figure of the Church, of which it is written: Your eyes are beautiful like a dove's (Song of Songs 1); and again our apostle Paul says of it: not having spot or wrinkle, or any such thing (Ephesians 5): its sight was clear and spiritual. For understand also how well what the apostle says in a mystery suits the Christian people: The first man, he says, is from the earth, earthly; but the second man is from heaven, heavenly (1 Corinthians 15). As is the earthly, such are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, such are the heavenly; and the law that is taken according to the letter kills, but the spirit gives life (2 Corinthians 3). For Moses, as we have mentioned, receiving the first tablets, threw them down broken, in order to show that your stony heart was broken and rejected, but that the heart of Christians was fit for the divine laws and to be kept. Hence Scripture says of the Christian people: Who show the work of the law written in their hearts (Romans 2). Knowing all these things, both from the law and the prophets, and considering still greater things, the holy apostle Paul separated himself from you, and would not bear the yoke with unbelievers; because there is no fellowship of light with darkness, nor portion of believer with unbeliever (2 Corinthians 6); he turned above all to Christ, because he had been admonished by him, that .... of belief ... ..... he should depart ..... the Christian people ........... ............. But the Jews say ........ ................................. the sign of salvation among us ...... in the sign of the Lord all, males and females alike, are signed; we are signed with the sign of the Lord on the forehead, as on the two doorposts, with the blood of the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, of whom it had already then been written in the law; which is recognised to have been fulfilled in the holy Gospel, when you shouted, saying: His blood be upon us and upon our children (Matthew 27). But it befits us to say this for our salvation: his blood be upon us and upon our children, for you to condemnation, but for us to salvation; because you say it with one purpose, we with another meaning; you raging, we praying; you insulting, we humbly beseeching; you out of hatred, we out of love; you as sorrowful, but we as always rejoicing. You chose the robber, because every animal turns to what is like itself; we have chosen to serve the Lord. We therefore, says the Apostle, are the Lord's; you followed the robber who reviled the Lord, we followed the robber who worshipped the Lord and confessed him on the cross: Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom. To whom the Lord said: Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23).
